segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been set in place by God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So whoever opposes the authority has resisted what God has set in place, and those who have resisted will bring judgment on themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For rulers are no cause of fear to good conduct, but to evil. Do you want to be unafraid of the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do what is evil, be afraid, for it does not carry the sword for nothing. It is God’s servant, an avenger who brings wrath on the one who practices evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of the wrath but also because of conscience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is also why you pay taxes, for the authorities are God’s public servants, devoting themselves to this very thing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pay everyone what you owe them: tax to the one owed tax, toll to the one owed toll, fear to the one owed fear, honor to the one owed honor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Owe no one anything, except to love one another, for the one who loves the other person has fulfilled the law.

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and any other commandment there may be, are summed up in this saying:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Love does no evil to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And do this knowing the time: it is already the hour for you to wake from sleep, for our salvation is nearer now than when we came to believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The night is far gone, and the day has drawn near. So let us throw off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let us walk decently, as in the day: not in carousing and drunkenness, not in promiscuity and debauchery, not in strife and jealousy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to satisfy its desires.

notes.note: The Greek is literally “every soul,” a Septuagint idiom in which the word simply designates an individual. Nothing is implied about an inner or immaterial part of a person. Most modern translations likewise have “every person” or “everyone.”

The phrase is literally “authorities that are over [one].” The great majority of scholars take it as the civil officials a resident of Rome would deal with, as the references to the sword and to taxes in verses 4–7 suggest. A minority view has held that angelic powers standing behind the state are also in view, since Paul elsewhere uses the same noun for spiritual powers.

notes.phrase: what God has set in place
notes.note: Verses 1–2 play on a single Greek word family: “be subject,” “set in place,” “opposes,” and this noun all share one root having to do with ordering or arranging. The noun means an arrangement or directive. It is rendered here to echo “set in place” in verse 1 so that some of the repetition survives in English.

The judgment could be the penalty imposed by the authorities themselves, or God’s judgment, or God’s judgment carried out through the authorities. The following verses, which speak of the ruler’s sword as an instrument of wrath, favor the last, but the Greek does not specify. The older rendering “damnation” says more than the word does.

The words “avenger” and “wrath” pick up 12:19, where readers were told not to avenge themselves but to leave room for the wrath, since vengeance belongs to God. Paul presents the ruler’s punishment of wrongdoing as one way that wrath is carried out. The chapter division obscures this connection.

This is a different word from “servant” in verse 4. In ordinary Greek it named someone who performed a public service or held a public office, and in the Septuagint it is also used of those serving in the temple. “Ministers” now suggests clergy or, in some countries, cabinet members. Whether Paul intends a sacred overtone here is debated.

notes.phrase: tax to the one owed tax, toll to the one owed toll
notes.traditional: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom
notes.note: Two kinds of payment are named. The first was the direct tax or tribute levied on subject peoples, and the second covered indirect charges such as customs duties and tolls on goods. Many modern translations have “taxes” and “revenue.”

notes.phrase: fear to the one owed fear
notes.traditional: respect to whom respect is owed
notes.note: The noun is the same one translated “fear” in verse 3, and it is kept here so the link is visible. Many modern translations soften it to “respect.” Some interpreters think Paul distinguishes fear, owed to God, from honor, owed to rulers, as in 1 Peter 2:17. Most take both as owed to human authorities of different rank.

notes.phrase: the one who loves the other person has fulfilled the law
notes.traditional: he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law
notes.note: The Greek could also be construed as “the one who loves has fulfilled the other law,” meaning the law of Moses as distinct from civil obligations. Nearly all translators and commentators take “the other” as the object of “loves,” as here, which fits the quotation about the neighbor in verse 9.

Manuscripts are divided between “you” and “us,” which differ by one letter in Greek. The edition translated here reads “you.” Many early and later witnesses read “us,” which matches “our salvation” in the next clause.

The edition translated here reads a verb meaning “throw off,” found in some early witnesses. Most manuscripts and most critical editions have a milder verb meaning “put off” or “lay aside,” which is Paul’s usual word for removing clothing in this kind of image. The sense is little affected.

The Greek word is literally “beds,” in the plural, a common euphemism for sexual intercourse; here it means illicit sexual encounters. “Sexual immorality” is avoided because it is the usual English for a different and broader Greek term.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the New Testament for authority, right, power and the powers (human and spiritual), and translations vary between “authority,” “power” and “right” in ways that hide connections.
Paul’s loaded use is rendered variously as “flesh,” “sinful nature” or “human nature,” and it needs one policy for the whole corpus.
Without the article and referring to the Mosaic commandments, it is unclear under house style whether to print “law” or “Law”; a ruling is needed for Paul’s letters.
The Semitic idiom for conduct is frequent in Paul and John, and translations split between “walk,” “live” and “behave.”
The word and its cognates range from civic office to priestly service (Romans 15:16; Philippians 2:25; Hebrews 8:2) and must be kept distinct from διάκονος and δοῦλος.
